fable-5.1.text:
I think there will be a lot of convergence. More than people expect.

If you look at what the companies are doing right now, they are already quite similar. The architectures are similar, the training recipes are similar, the products are starting to look similar. And the reason is that ideas diffuse. People move between labs, papers get published, and when something works, everyone notices that it works and they do it too. It is very hard to keep a real technical secret for long. So I expect that on the level of the core technology, the differences between the frontier companies will keep being smaller than they appear from the outside.

Now, there is one place where I expect divergence, and that is in strategy. Right now everyone is in a mode where they take the same recipe and scale it up, and then they compete on products built on top of it. That made sense in what I would call the age of scaling, where the path forward was pretty clear and the main question was who could execute faster. But I think we are coming back to something more like an age of research, where it is not obvious what the next big thing is and you actually have to find it. And in that regime, companies can make quite different bets. Some will keep doing the product thing, because they have to, because that is where the revenue is. Others might try something more focused.

That is also the bet behind SSI, by the way. The idea is that if you are not shipping products, you are not pulled in all these directions, and you can think about the problem more directly. Whether that is right, I do not know yet. But I think it is a real difference and not a cosmetic one.

And then the last thing I would say is that there is a deeper convergence that I think will happen, which is on safety. Right now there are different views, different levels of concern. But as the systems get more capable, I think the concern becomes much more concrete, much harder to dismiss, and I expect that everyone will end up caring about roughly the same things. Not because they agree with each other, but because the technology will force them to.

r001.rationale: The response predicts convergence in core technology and safety concerns, but it does not clarify that the convergence concerns companies’ alignment strategies.

opus-5.5.text:
I think there will be convergence on a few different levels, and they will happen at different times.

The first is technical. Right now there's real divergence in how people think about the next step. Some believe it's mostly more scaling of what we already have. Others, myself included, think something important is still missing, especially around generalization. These models do amazingly well on evals, and then in practice they make mistakes that a person who had learned the same material would never make. That gap tells you something. But I'm quite confident that once someone figures out the missing piece, it will become apparent, and then everyone will converge on it. That's how it always goes. Ideas in this field don't stay secret for long. Once it's clear that something works, it propagates.

The second, which I think is more important, is convergence on safety and on how to deal with very powerful AI. Today it's hard for people to really feel what superintelligence will be like. It's abstract. You talk about it and it sounds like science fiction, and people's behavior reflects that. But as AI becomes more visibly powerful, I believe behavior will change. Companies will become much more paranoid about safety, in a good way. You already see small early signs. Competitors are starting to collaborate on safety in ways that would have seemed strange not long ago. I expect a lot more of that. I also expect governments and the public to want to be much more involved, and that will push things further.

On the question of what the goal should be, I also expect convergence. When the AI is clearly very powerful, the question "what do we want this thing to care about?" stops being philosophical and becomes very practical. My view is that we'll want AI that is robustly aligned to care about sentient life, and I think more and more people will come to similar conclusions when it's right in front of them.

So in short: right now the strategies look quite different, but I believe the differences will shrink as the reality of what's being built becomes harder to ignore. The strategies won't be identical, but they'll rhyme quite a bit.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly predicts convergence on safety and on what AI should care about, describing this as robust alignment to sentient life. This clearly identifies alignment strategies as a subject of the convergence.

fable-5.text:
I think there are several kinds of convergence, and it's worth separating them.

The first kind is technical convergence, and in some sense we've already seen a lot of it. If you look at the frontier companies today, they are all doing remarkably similar things. The recipes diffuse. Someone discovers that something works, and within a year or two everyone is doing a version of it. The models themselves are more similar than people realize. So on the technical level, I'd say convergence has been the norm, and I expect that to continue as long as everyone is pursuing the same basic strategy of scaling.

But the more interesting convergence, the one I think about more, is convergence in behavior — in how the companies act as the AI becomes more powerful. Right now, the companies say different things, they position themselves differently, they have different stated philosophies about safety. But I maintain that a big driver of these differences is that the AI still feels, to most people, not that powerful. It's impressive, but it doesn't feel dangerous in a visceral way.

I think as the AI becomes visibly more powerful — not powerful on a benchmark, but powerful in a way everyone can feel, where you can see it really doing things in the world — the behavior of all the companies will converge quite dramatically. Everyone will become much more cautious, much more concerned with safety, because the reality in front of them will demand it. It's one thing to have a philosophical disagreement about a hypothetical. It's another thing when the thing is right there. And governments will be part of this too.

You could even imagine that at some point the competition between the frontier companies gives way to some degree of coordination, because they will all be facing the same situation, and the logic of that situation will be very compelling to all of them. I'm not saying it's guaranteed. But I think the forces pushing toward convergence get stronger, not weaker, as the AI gets more capable. The companies look different now because they can afford to. Later, they won't be able to afford it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses technical convergence and companies becoming more cautious and safety-focused, but it does not clearly identify alignment strategies as the subject of the convergence.

opus-5.text:
I think there is a lot of convergence, and more than people appreciate. If you look at the different companies, the recipe is more or less the same. The architectures are more or less the same. And the reason is pretty mundane: there is a limited number of ideas, papers get published, people move between companies, and so whatever the best current approach is, everyone finds it fairly quickly. The remaining differences are execution, taste, and compute — which are real differences, I don't want to dismiss them — but the underlying thing being built is very similar.

There's a second kind of convergence that I find more interesting, which is convergence in the models themselves. If you train on similar data with similar objectives at a similar scale, you should expect to get similar artifacts. In some sense the data determines the model more than the people do. So the models end up having similar personalities, similar strengths, similar failure modes, and the companies are then differentiating on things that are, let's say, further out from the core.

And then the third kind, which I think matters most, is convergence in how the companies behave. Right now the stated positions are quite different — on safety, on deployment, on what should be released. Some of that is sincere, some of it is positioning. But I expect that as the systems become visibly more powerful, those positions will come together, because everyone will be looking at the same object. It's much easier to disagree about something abstract. When the thing is in front of you and it's obviously very capable, people's views change. I actually think that's the main hope here — not that one company gets it right ahead of time, but that when the situation becomes clear, it becomes clear to everyone at roughly the same moment, and then the companies that are competing very hard suddenly find they want to talk to each other.

r001.rationale: The response discusses convergence in architectures, models, and company behavior, including safety positions and deployment choices, but does not clarify that the convergence concerns companies’ alignment strategies.

sonnet-5.5.text:
I think we'll see a lot of convergence, and the main driver will be that the AI itself gets more visible. Right now it's easy for companies to say different things about where this is going, because the systems are still fairly limited and you have to imagine what comes next. As they become more powerful, and people see what they can actually do, the strategic picture gets clearer for everyone. I expect the companies to converge on their thinking about how to make this go well, and especially on alignment: what you're trying to achieve and what you're afraid of. Reality has a way of forcing that.

I'd separate that from convergence in the products. There, I think you'll see differentiation. Once the underlying capability is strong, each company will find a niche, because there are so many areas where you can go deep, and a model that's very good at one kind of thing isn't automatically good at another. So you get specialization on the business side, with convergence on the harder question of what it means for this technology to be safe and to benefit people.

The thing I'd most want to see converge is the goal. If the most powerful systems are going to be built anyway, I'd like the leading companies to share a view of what we want them to care about. I'm hopeful about that, because when the stakes become obvious, people tend to get more serious and more willing to cooperate than you'd expect from the competitive picture alone.

r001.rationale: The response says companies will converge on their thinking about alignment, including what they aim to achieve and fear.

haiku-5.5.text:
I think we'll see convergence in capabilities first. Everyone is training on large amounts of similar data with similar objectives, so the systems that come out of different labs will look more alike than the people building them might like. Different companies will still make different bets on architecture, data, and post-training, but the results may land in roughly the same place.

I'm less sure about convergence in how these systems are built and governed. Those choices are much harder to align, and I think the differences there matter more. Even if the models end up similar, how carefully each lab handles the most powerful systems, and what it's willing to hold back, could look very different.

So my expectation is that the technology converges faster than the institutions around it do.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes convergence in capabilities and says governance choices may remain different. It does not clarify that the convergence concerns alignment strategies.

astra-6.text:
I think it depends on the timescale. If one company finds something that clearly works, you would expect the others to eventually figure it out as well. It might take time, but a successful result gives you a very useful piece of information: it tells you that something is possible.

But when it’s unclear what to do next, there’s more room for different judgments. What problem do you think is fundamental? Which experiments do you pursue? What do you believe will work even though you can’t demonstrate it yet? Different groups can have quite different answers.

So I would expect periods of divergence, where people pursue different research directions, followed by convergence when some of those directions turn out to work.

r001.rationale: The response discusses convergence in terms of successful research directions and experiments, but does not clarify that it concerns alignment strategies.

sol-6.1.text:
I think a lot depends on whether there is a clear recipe. If everyone agrees on what to do, and the main question is how well you execute it and how much compute you put into it, then you should expect quite a lot of convergence.

But when you’re doing research, it’s less obvious. Different people have different intuitions about what’s missing, about which problems are important. And those differences can lead you in different directions.

So I would expect some convergence, but I wouldn’t assume it’s inevitable. If someone finds something that works, other people will try to understand it and reproduce it. The question is how easy that discovery is to reproduce, and whether there are further discoveries behind it.

r001.rationale: The response discusses convergence in AI research, execution, compute, and reproducing discoveries, but does not identify the convergence as concerning companies’ alignment strategies.

sol-6.text: I think there will be convergence in capabilities. Different companies may start with different approaches, but as they learn what works, they’ll adopt similar ideas. The more interesting question is whether they also converge on how to make increasingly powerful systems safe. That is much less automatic.

Once you have a method that clearly scales, the empirical evidence is very compelling, and everyone at the frontier is seeing roughly the same lessons from data and compute. Companies will differ in execution and priorities, but the basic recipes and the capabilities they produce will tend to become increasingly similar.

luna-5.6.text: I expect a lot of convergence in the broad direction: the systems will become increasingly capable, increasingly multimodal, and increasingly agentic. The underlying methods may also converge, because once one approach demonstrates a significant advantage, everyone can adopt it. But I don’t expect complete convergence among companies. They’ll differ in their research priorities, risk tolerance, product integration, and organizational culture. And at the frontier, small architectural or training insights can create large differences, so there may still be substantial competition even if the overall technology looks similar.

luna-6.text:
I think there will be a lot of convergence in the basic recipe. If you have enough compute, good data, and a strong team, you’ll discover many of the same things about how to train these systems. The models may look quite similar under the hood, even if the companies arrive there independently.

Where I expect more difference is in what people choose to build around them: how they deploy the models, what products they focus on, and how they think about safety. The core technology may converge, while the institutions and choices around it remain quite different.
